newsitem.title: FRANCE: Renault has no comment on loss report.
newsitem.headline: Renault has no comment on loss report.

text.p: French carmaker Renault SA, struggling against persistent weakness in the European car market, declined on Wednesday to comment on a press report it would post a 1996 net loss of four to five billion francs ($709 to $887 million).
"The accounts are not consolidated yet. We can make no comment before March 20" when the company is due to announce its results, a Renault spokesman said.
French financial daily Les Echos, citing a company source, said Renault's net loss would total between "four and five billion francs". The loss would be Renault's first in 10 years.
The source was quoted as saying that the loss would take into account restructuring costs which the newspaper said were expected to be massive.

Renault, hit by sluggish sales and a savage price war, reported a 41 percent drop in 1995 net attributable profit to 2.14 billion francs. First half profits slid to 158 million francs from 1.76 billion a year earlier.
Renault shares, which have been losing ground amid deepening gloom over the carmaker's outlook, were down 1.16 percent at 119.60 francs in early afternoon.
The shares were sold to retail investors for 165 francs in the first leg of the group's privatisation in 1994.
Renault warned earlier this month that its operating loss would be considerably higher than market forecasts.

Les Echos said analysts had already boosted their expectations for 1996 operating losses to two to 2.5 billion francs, up from earlier estimates of 1.3 billion to 1.6 billion francs, after the company sounded the alarm on February 14.

Renault chairman Louis Schweitzer said last September the company would probably end the year in the red as cost-cutting efforts were unlikely to offset the weakness in the European car market and the price competion which has eroded profit margins.
The company has said it expects to lose money on both its car and truck operations this year. Only its financial operations are expected to be in the black, Les Echos said.
French car sales fell 34 percent in January, underscoring the market's weakness after more than two years of state support through incentives for people to buy new vehicles.
The incentives ended last September. ($= 5.637 French Francs)
